data.title: Klapy – a Celtic hillfort above the Nosice reservoir
data.excerpt: The craggy ridge of Klapy, also called Klapé or Cigánka, is one of the natural landmarks of the upper Váh region, rising above the Nosice reservoir between the villages of Udiča, Uhry and Šebešťanová. Its summit was occupied as early as the Hallstatt period and later by the people of the Púchov culture; the finds from the hill include bronze bracelets, a brooch in the shape of a horse and hoards of Celtic coins.

children.text: The hill of Klapy (or Klapé, or else Cigánka) is one of the natural landmarks of the upper Váh region and is visible from afar to anyone travelling by rail or by car off the motorway between Púchov and Považská Bystrica. It lies between the villages of Udiča, Uhry and Šebešťanová.

blocks.caption: A splendid bronze brooch in the shape of a horse
blocks.alt: A splendid bronze brooch in the shape of a horse

children.text: It is formed by a craggy ridge above the Nosice reservoir, built of limestones and calcareous sandstones with a varied mosaic of plant and animal species, which is divided into Malé Klapy and Veľké Klapy. It is part of the Klippen Belt and has been declared a nature reserve. From the hillfort there is an excellent view over the valley of the Váh and the wider surroundings, and it has direct visual contact with several contemporary hillforts (for example Malý Manín or the other defences mentioned below). A waymarked path leads to its summit.
Some historians judge that the name Klapy is at least two thousand years old (its origin may lie in the Germanic word for rock –
). Others (for example Meliš in the book Po stopách predkov – In the Footsteps of Our Ancestors) consider the name Klape to be Celtic.

Klapy was occupied on its summit as early as the period of the Hallstatt culture and subsequently by the population of the Púchov culture in the time of the Celts. The northern slope of Klapy is not as sheer as the southern side, but it is steep as well. A number of narrow terraces were laid out here, which were inhabited in the Roman period, but sherds from the time of the Migration Period (5th century) were also found here, and even sherds of the Early Middle Ages. The terraces lie at several altitudinal levels of the hill and are hard to reach up the steep slope of Klapy. There is good reason to assume that Klapy was fortified, and Dr Karol Pieta describes it as an old Hallstatt hillfort which was later used by the people of the Púchov culture. A few hundred metres from Klapy there are two further sets of defences, namely the small fort of the Púchov culture at Jasenica – Predná hôrka and the extensive Hradište, occupied not only around the turn of the era but also in the Great Moravian period.

Among the first known metal finds is an iron knife, beside which La Tène pottery lay; later stone whetstones were found, as well as a mould for casting small bronze spirals, made of sandstone. A Celtic spur, brooches and fragments of them and other smaller metal finds are also known.

children.text: With the spread of metal detectors, very valuable finds began to be made on Klapy, but these often ended up in private hands and we know nothing about them. Some exceptional finds that have been published in the specialist literature are, however, known. Among the most valuable are, for example, bronze bracelets with mouldings from the end of the Hallstatt period. Exceptional finds are also a bronze figurine of a bull and an extraordinarily beautiful bronze brooch in the shape of a horse.

children.text:
Klapy has also yielded finds of Celtic silver and gold coins, both singly and as part of mass finds – coin hoards. Some of them have been published, such as a coin of the Veľký Bysterec type or the coin hoard found in 2000, which contained 57 silver coins with abstract symbols, 6 gold staters and silver tetradrachms. These finds prove that Klapy and its surroundings were of great importance in antiquity and were inhabited by well-to-do people. They form part of the dense occupation around Púchov, Udiča, Prosné, Jasenica and the Váh. Below the defences there are several open settlements of the Hallstatt period and of the Púchov culture, and it is likely that Klapy served as a refuge for the inhabitants of these settlements.
 
 Orgoň
